body: Beneish (1999) 8-variable model: M = -4.84 + 0.92*DSRI + 0.528*GMI + 0.404*AQI + 0.892*SGI + 0.115*DEPI - 0.172*SGAI + 4.679*TATA - 0.327*LVGI. DSRI = receivable-days index (Ricoh, Cox & Kings); GMI = gross-margin deterioration; AQI = asset quality (non-current assets ex-PP&E growing = capitalisation); SGI = sales growth (high growth raises pressure); DEPI = slowing depreciation; SGAI = SG&A index; TATA = total accruals to assets ((PAT - CFO)/assets) -- the heaviest weight, i.e., profit not backed by cash; LVGI = leverage index. Cut-offs: M > -1.78 = likely manipulator (the threshold for the 8-variable model per Beneish 1999 / Beneish-Lee-Nichols 2013); < -2.22 is commonly used as 'unlikely' (the 5-variable variant / practitioner convention); grey zone between. Base rates: the FAJ 1999 version reported the model identified roughly half of manipulators before public discovery; the often-quoted '76% detected with 17.5% false positives' is for a specific cut-off/error-cost assumption -- treat as unverified. Cornell students flagged Enron in 1998. Limits: not for banks/NBFCs/insurers; noisy for high-growth firms (SGI); one-year snapshot -- trend matters; it flags earnings management, not fraud proof. Use as a filter to trigger deeper work, never as a sole signal.
title: Beneish M-score: cut-offs, components, base rates

body: Cohen, Malloy and Nguyen (J. Finance 75(3), 2020; NBER w25084) compared each firm's 10-K/10-Q text with its previous filing, 1995-2014. Firms that changed their reports ('changers') subsequently underperformed. A short-changers / long-non-changers portfolio earned up to 188 bp/month (about 22%/yr) when changes were in the risk-factor section; broader value-weighted spreads were about 34-58 bp/month. Changes about the CEO/CFO, litigation and more negative wording were the most predictive. There was no announcement-day reaction. Returns built up over as long as 18 months as the news later surfaced, and did not reverse, which means investors simply don't read the diffs. Application to India: diff each annual report (MD&A, risk, contingent liabilities, related-party notes, auditor's report and CARO) and each concall against the prior year's. Flag unusually large changes, new risk language and dropped KPIs. Indian small caps are even less read than US filers, so the inattention premium is plausibly larger, though that is untested in India. Effect sizes come from the abstract and digest.
title: Lazy Prices: year-on-year changes in filing text predict returns (Cohen-Malloy-Nguyen 2020)

body: DTA on carried-forward losses needs 'convincing evidence' of future profit (Ind AS 12); recognising it is a non-cash PAT boost. SUZLON (Screener): PBT 1,447 / PAT 2,072 in FY25 (ETR -43%), PBT 2,422 / PAT 3,163 in FY26 (ETR -31%) - ~Rs1,366 cr of PAT over two years from tax credits; normalised FY26 PAT at ~25% tax is ~1,800, so a P/E on 3,163 overstates earnings power ~75% (derived from Screener lines; confirm DTA note). HINDUNILVR FY26 ETR fell 26% -> 17% because the ~Rs4,611 cr ice-cream demerger gain was largely untaxed. Other causes: India's FY20 move to 25.17% (s.115BAA) DTA remeasurement, SEZ/holiday expiry, uncertain tax positions. Rule: value on PBT x normalised rate (India 25.17%; US 21% + state); treat ETR <15% or >35% as non-representative unless structural. Exercise: PBT +7% with ETR 25% -> 9% shows PAT +30%; true growth +7%.
title: Deferred-tax recognition and tax-rate swings inflate PAT (Suzlon FY25-26, HUL FY26)
